html:
The Napo Kichwa, or Napo Runa, are a Kichwa-speaking people of the Napo River valley in the Amazon lowlands of Ecuador and northern Peru. Their language is a lowland form of Quechua, which spread here partly through trade with the Andes and later as a mission language.

In 1541 Francisco de Orellana floated down the Napo on the journey that took him along the whole Amazon. Spanish rule followed, and in 1578 the peoples of the Quijos and upper Napo rose in a great revolt that was crushed. Later came Jesuit missions and the rubber boom, and from the 1960s oil drilling and roads. The Napo Kichwa farm, fish and hunt along the river, and many now run community tourism. See also Amazonian Kichwa.
